Before you start

Students learn that friendships run on hours together and that people like us more than we guess, then pick one thing that repeats. Bring index cards, don't ask who's new or why anyone moved, and give students who aren't new a way to add hours for someone who is.

Every student in the room

For students who share their race, faith or home language with few others here, "do I belong?" can be louder; point to repeat places that cost nothing, like a job, a faith group or a free club.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Open plainly: some of you are new, some remember what month one felt like. Don’t ask who’s new.

Slide 2 · Notes

Everyone guesses a number first. Then eyes closed, hands up, and you count out loud. The next slide is what usually happens.

Slide 3 · Notes

If the room guessed low, say it. If the guess matched, say so and move on.

Slide 4 · Notes

Ask: “Where are you with most people here?” In your head.

Slide 5 · Notes

Say it out loud: you haven’t logged the hours yet.

Slide 6 · Notes

Small talk alone was linked to drifting apart.

Slide 7 · Notes

Ask: “Why do we guess low?” We replay our own awkward moments. They didn’t notice them.

Slide 8 · Notes

Two minutes in pairs, then a few answers. Expect: asking about something they mentioned, sitting at the same table.

Slide 9 · Notes

Specific is easier to say yes to than “we should hang out sometime.”

Slide 10 · Notes

Partners by seat: what would you try? A few answers, then the next slide.

Slide 11 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 12 · Notes

Partners decide. More than one answer works. The next slide shows one good one.

Slide 13 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 14 · Notes

Keep the talk on what classmates can do, never on his English or his background. The next slide shows one good move.

Slide 15 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 16 · Notes

Private: “Where could your first hours come from?” Repeat places that cost nothing count.

Slide 17 · Notes

Turn and talk, partners by seat. Then ask: “Where else in your life does this show up?” Nobody speaks for a group.

Slide 18 · Notes

Pick one in your head, and when you’ll start. Share the take-home link.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why friendships take time (they run on hours together), use the liking gap to act on the better guess after an awkward conversation, and pick one thing that repeats. Students who aren't new pick one way to add hours for someone who is.

Materials

  • Index cards: one per student, for the anonymous guess and the private plan
  • A board or sheet of paper for the tally
  • The student page link (last slide) to share after advisory

Flow

  1. 3 minThe guess (anonymous cards)
  2. 4 minFriendship runs on hours
  3. 3 minThe liking gap (pair-share)
  4. 3 minMore hours, better hours
  5. 4 minThree moments (scenario talk)
  6. 3 minOne thing that repeats (private card) and the link

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

The guess and the tally (3), friendship runs on hours (3), the liking gap (2), one thing that repeats and the link (2).

Before you teach
Don't ask who's new.

Some students arrived this fall, and some have been at Beaver for years. Don't ask for a show of hands or put a new student on the spot to talk about it. The guess on slide 2 works for everyone, including seniors remembering their first month.

Lonely is close to the surface.

Someone in your circle may be eating lunch alone most days. Never ask who has a group or who they sit with. If a student seems isolated, check in privately afterward and loop in a counselor.

Don't ask why anyone moved.

Students change schools for all kinds of reasons: a job, a divorce, a death, a new home, immigration, a hard year somewhere else. The lesson is about what helps now.

Being left out on purpose is different.

If a student is being targeted or excluded because of their race, religion, accent, or where they're from, that is a counselor or dean conversation that day, not a discussion topic.

Know when it's more than new.

Dreading school most mornings, feeling sick before coming, still feeling alone most of the time after a couple of months, or big changes in sleep, eating or mood are reasons to see a counselor. Don't ask about these in advisory. Any disclosure goes to a counselor the same day, and 988 is there any time.

Old friends are a real support.

Don't frame old friends as something to drop. The goal is keeping some time open for new hours to happen.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Being one of few here from your background.

For students who share their race, culture, faith or home language with few others at Beaver, "do I belong here?" can be louder. That isn't proof they're in the wrong place. Name affinity groups and clubs, and say it's fair to expect the school to make room. Don't ask anyone to speak for their group.

Moving from another country.

The unwritten rules at a new school can be different, and accents and home languages get noticed. The student page says plainly that erasing your background, accent or faith to fit in costs more than it buys. Keep the Nico scenario on what classmates can do, never on Nico's English.

"Join something weekly" can cost money and rides.

Some teams and activities need fees, gear, or a ride home late. Some students work or care for siblings after school. A job counts as weekly hours, and a library study plan or a lunch table is free.

Faith can be the weekly thing, or can shape the week.

A youth group or faith community counts as repeated hours with the same people. Some students can't go out on certain nights for faith or family reasons. Lunch and school-day options work for them too.

Small talk is harder for some students.

For autistic students and students with social anxiety, "one question past small talk" can take real effort. Activities with a shared task, like a robotics build, a show crew or a team, give conversation something to hang on. Don't make outgoing the measure of fitting in.

"Find one adult" may matter more for some.

Students who moved for a family change, live in foster or kinship care, or don't have an adult at home who can drive them to things may lean on a school adult more. Make sure every student leaves knowing at least one adult at Beaver they could go to.

What the research says

Adults who had just moved and first-year college students estimated it took about 50 hours together to go from acquaintance to casual friend, about 90 to become friends, and more than 200 for a close friend. Students got there faster than adults. These are rough averages from people's own estimates.

Hall, Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 2019

Hanging out, joking around and real conversations counted most toward closeness. Sitting near each other in class or working side by side counted less, and small talk alone was linked to drifting apart.

Hall, 2019

People who had just talked with someone new consistently underestimated how much the other person liked them. It showed up in first-year college roommates and lasted for months.

Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom and Clark, Psychological Science, 2018

Commuters asked to talk to a stranger on a train or bus reported a more pleasant ride than those who sat alone, though people predicted the opposite. The mistake came from underestimating how interested others are in connecting.

Epley and Schroeder, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2014

First-year college students who read that belonging worries are common and fade went on to earn higher grades over three years if they were Black, cutting the racial achievement gap in half. It was a small study.

Walton and Cohen, Science, 2011

Repeated with almost 27,000 students at 22 colleges, a version under 30 minutes helped more students finish their first year full time, especially in groups that had historically struggled more, but only at schools that offered real ways to belong.

Walton et al., Science, 2023
